latin.533: Adde quod Apostolus probat hoc loco omnes homines esse peccatores, peccatum in mundo, id est in hominibus, hoc argumento, quod omnes moriuntur. Putasne probare eum peccatum esse in hominibus, quia sit in hominibus peccatum, nimirum corruptio haereditaria? Num a latente corruptione morali, quae ipsa erat probanda, ducit argumentum, cum suppeteret a patente & nota omnium morte?
latin.534: Certe condemnatio & mors sunt apud Apostolum hoc capite correlata. Condemnamur ad mortem, non ad peccatum. Mors non est condemnationis causa, sed effectum. Contra peccatum (est autem corruptio haereditaria, ut iam saepius dixi, peccatum) condemnationis causa, non effectum.
latin.535: Denique, ut ne sim aequo prolixior, cum ait Apostolus vers. 21. regnasse peccatum in mortem, sitne verisimile alio modo accipi mortem, quam in antecedenti disputatione Apostoli, cuius versus ille conclusio est? At profecto eo versu id significare non potest, quod sit vere peccatum. Praecessit enim illud vers. 20. lex praeterea introiit, ut peccatum abundaret. ubi autem peccatum abundavit, ibi gratia superabundavit. Illud enim peccati regnum, haec peccati redundantia id omne in homine complectitur, quod vere peccatum sit, & liquet ex Rom. VI. & VII. id peccatum, quod per legem redundavit & regnavit, esse concupiscentiam, sive corruptionem haereditariam.
latin.536: Putabis fortasse te horum argumentorum aciem declinare posse, dicendo, per peccatum τὴν ἁμαρτίαν intelligi utrumque & peccatum actuale Adami, & natum ex eo vitium originale; sed id tibi non licet per statum quaestionis, quae inter nos versatur. Est enim instituta de peccato actuali Adami praeciso a vitio haereditario. Vis enim primum peccatum actuale Adamo & nobis fuisse imputatum, & quia imputatum, inflictam Adamo & nobis hanc poenam, nimirum vitium seu corruptionem originalem. Itaque secundum tuam sententiam corruptio ista cum peccato actuali Adami non cohaeret, nisi divinae imputationis interventu. Quare imputatio naturae ordine corruptionem antecedit. Est igitur peccati actualis Adami praecisi a corruptione haereditaria imputatio tibi probanda, non autem cum ea coniuncti ac confusi.
latin.537: Id quod mihi alia suggerit argumenta, sed, vitandae hoc loco nimiae prolixitatis causa, conferenda in alium locum. Adde quod iam probavi peccatum actuale non introiisse in mundum, hoc est, in homines: unde sequitur hoc attributum in mundum introiit sibi iungere peccatum, non qua significat peccatum actuale, sed qua significat vitium ex eo mea sententia immediate, tua vero mediante Dei imputatione ortum. Sic opinor meum argumentum firmavi satis.
latin.538: Vides prima verba Apostoli, quae sequentium sunt basis; at eorum saltem nullius vestigium deprehendo in tuo tractatu. Quid si ego inde aliquid eliciam sententiae tuae adversum. Dabisne mihi per mortem hoc loco intelligendam esse eam mortem, quam lex Adamo fuerat comminata, poenam scilicet, & stipendium peccati? non video quo iure id negare possis, praesertim cum sentias eam legem ad totum genus humanum spectare, & Adamum, prout Deus minatus fuerat, mortuum esse. Dabis saltem mortem hoc loco significare poenam peccati, quod in mundum introiit.

pass_a.533: Add: Paul proves here that all humans are sinners—sin in the world, that is, in humans—by this argument, that all die. Do you think he proves sin is in humans because hereditary corruption is in humans—the very thing to be proved? Does he argue from a latent moral corruption when the open, known death of all was at hand?
pass_a.534: Certainly in this chapter condemnation and death are correlatives for Paul. We are condemned to death, not to sin. Death is not condemnation's cause but its effect. Sin—by which I mean hereditary corruption, as I have often said—is condemnation's cause, not its effect.
pass_a.535: Not to run on: when Paul says (v. 21) sin reigned unto death, is it likely 'death' means something else than in the preceding dispute of which that verse is the close? It cannot there mean what is truly sin. Verse 20 came first: the law entered that sin might abound; where sin abounded, grace superabounded. That reign and overflow of sin covers all that is truly sin in a human—and from Rom 6–7 it is clear the sin that overflowed and reigned through the law is concupiscence, or hereditary corruption.
pass_a.536: You may think to blunt these strokes by saying τὴν ἁμαρτίαν means both Adam's actual and the original vice born from it—but the status of our question forbids that. It is set about Adam's actual cut from hereditary vice. You will have the first actual imputed to Adam and to us, and because imputed, this penalty inflicted— namely original vice/corruption. So on your view that corruption coheres with Adam's actual only by divine imputation intervening. Hence imputation precedes corruption in the order of nature. You must prove imputation of Adam's actual cut from hereditary corruption—not of the two joined and confused.
pass_a.537: That suggests further arguments, which for brevity I put elsewhere. Add that I have already proved actual did not enter the world—that is, into humans: so the attribute 'entered into the world' joins itself to sin not as it means bare actual, but as it means the vice sprung from it (immediately on my view; by God's imputation on yours). So I think my argument stands firm enough.
pass_a.538: You see Paul's first words, the basis of what follows; yet I find no trace of them in your treatise. What if I draw from them something against your view? Will you grant that by death here is meant the death the law had threatened Adam—penalty and wages of sin? I do not see by what right you can deny it, especially when you hold that law regards the whole race, and Adam died as God had threatened. At least grant death here means the penalty of the sin that entered the world. Tip before ἐφ' ᾧ / ἐφ' ᾧ πάντες.

533: Add that the Apostle proves in this place that all humans are sinners, that sin is in the world, that is in humans, by this argument, that all die. Do you think he proves that sin is in humans, because there is sin in humans, namely hereditary corruption? Does he draw the argument from a latent moral corruption, which itself was to be proved, when it was at hand from the open and known death of all?
534: Certainly condemnation and death are correlatives with the Apostle in this chapter. We are condemned to death, not to sin. Death is not the cause of condemnation, but the effect. On the contrary sin (but hereditary corruption is sin, as I have already often said) is the cause of condemnation, not the effect.
535: Finally, that I may not be too prolix, when the Apostle says in verse 21. that sin reigned unto death, is it likely that death is taken in another way than in the Apostle's preceding dispute, of which that verse is the conclusion? But surely in that verse it cannot signify that which is truly sin. For that preceded in verse 20. the law moreover entered, that sin might abound. But where sin abounded, there grace superabounded. For that reign of sin, this overflow of sin, embraces all that in a human which is truly sin, and it is clear from Rom. VI. and VII. that that sin which overflowed and reigned through the law is concupiscence, or hereditary corruption.
536: You will perhaps think you can turn aside the edge of these arguments by saying that by sin, ten hamartian, both are understood, both Adam's actual sin, and the original vice born from it; but that is not allowed you by the status of the question which is treated between us. For it is instituted concerning Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary vice. For you will have the first actual sin to have been imputed to Adam and to us, and because imputed, this penalty to have been inflicted on Adam and on us, namely original vice or corruption. And so according to your opinion that corruption does not cohere with Adam's actual sin except by the intervention of divine imputation. Wherefore imputation in the order of nature precedes corruption. Therefore the imputation of Adam's actual sin cut off from hereditary corruption must be proved by you, not however of it joined and confused with that.
537: Which suggests other arguments to me, but, for the sake of avoiding too much prolixity in this place, to be conferred to another place. Add that I have already proved that actual sin did not enter into the world, that is, into humans: whence it follows that this attribute entered into the world joins sin to itself, not insofar as it signifies actual sin, but insofar as it signifies the vice arisen from it in my opinion immediately, but in yours by the mediation of God's imputation. So I think I have confirmed my argument enough.
538: You see the Apostle's first words, which are the basis of those that follow; but of them at least I detect no vestige in your treatise. What if I from there elicit something adverse to your opinion. Will you grant me that by death in this place is to be understood that death which the law had threatened to Adam, namely the penalty, and the wages of sin? I do not see by what right you can deny that, especially since you hold that that law regards the whole human race, and that Adam, as God had threatened, died. You will at least grant that death in this place signifies the penalty of the sin which entered into the world.
